walkthroughs.body_html:
Biological Resources — a core area of A-Level Environmental Science.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Biological Resources brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Biological Resources.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Who argued food can't keep up with population (1798)?
options: Darwin
Malthus
Marx
Smith

mcqs.q: Shift from high to low birth/death rates is called?
options: Demographic transition
Carrying capacity
Population pyramid
Mortality crisis

mcqs.q: What does the 'tragedy of the commons' describe?
options: Fertiliser makes the water too acidic.
It is a play about poor people.
Shared resources tend to be overexploited because individuals benefit personally while sharing costs.
Common land in medieval Britain.

mcqs.q: How does fertiliser runoff cause aquatic dead zones?
options: Fertiliser directly poisons fish.
Excess nutrients fuel algal blooms; when algae die, decomposition depletes water oxygen.
Common land in medieval Britain.
Fertiliser makes the water too acidic.

mcqs.q: Why does renewable energy require energy storage solutions?
options: Solar and wind generation are intermittent - storage smooths out supply and demand.
Fertiliser makes the water too acidic.
Because they generate too much energy.
Renewable energy can never meet demand.
